source.title: Surgical Refusal Ablation: Disentangling Safety from Intelligence via Concept-Guided Spectral Cleaning

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper examines entanglement in refusal-ablation directions, not superposition of model features, capacity competition, SAE features, or feature dimensionality as specified by the claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper's refusal-ablation outcomes and capability perplexities do not test the listed versions. Its directly relevant adjacent result is that a contrastive refusal vector overlaps with capability/style atoms; this is a different construct from feature superposition or polysemantic neurons.
record.test_reason: The paper calls a contrastive refusal vector 'polysemantic' because it overlaps with concept-atom directions built from contrastive prompts. It does not study superposition of features in neurons or toy models. It also does not study capacity, SAE dictionary features, or feature dimensionality. Its results evaluate a refusal-ablation method. The direction-overlap finding is a different construct from any listed version.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that the raw refusal vector entangles refusal with capability and style directions. They report that SRA residualization achieves 0–2% refusal with far lower first-token KL drift than standard ablation, and that it preserves or improves GSM8K/MBPP perplexity. They attribute standard-ablation damage to this entanglement ('Ghost Noise').
record.recipe_differences: The study uses concept-atom residualization followed by rank-one weight updates for refusal ablation; it does not reproduce the toy-network feature-superposition method.
record.method_sensitivity: The paper reports different refusal-reduction outcomes across tested models and methods; its iterative spectral analysis is shown for Qwen3-VL-2B at Layer 25.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen3-VL-2B, the mean-difference refusal direction has cosine about -0.22 with a Logic atom and +0.18 with a Coding atom. Residualizing against Shield/Confound atoms reduces their projection on the intervention direction.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Contrastive steering directions (e.g., refusal) overlap with other contrastively defined capability/style directions, and removing that overlap reduces collateral drift of the edit.

record.problems: The atom registry is curated and may miss confounds, as the authors note. The cited cosine values are approximate, and the projection comparison is qualitative in the text. The paper also notes finite harmful-prompt suites, definition-dependent refusal detection, and that perplexity and first-token KL are proxies rather than comprehensive behavioral evaluations.
record.rows_left_out: No refusal-rate, distribution-drift, or math/code perplexity rows were included: those evaluate the refusal-ablation intervention and its collateral effects, not any listed claim version or the adjacent vector-overlap finding.

untested.parts: Toy networks, sparsity-dependent transition, and geometry of superposed features
Capacity competition as the cause of neuron polysemanticity
Polysemantic neurons arising without capacity pressure
Feature spread across LLM neurons, and SAE recovery of sparse features
Completeness, stability, or canonicity of SAE features

record.verdict_notes: The paper uses 'polysemantic' loosely, for a steering vector rather than neurons, and does not engage superposition theory or cite the original source. The R² of the atom regression is only about 3.5% at pass 1, so atoms explain little of the refusal vector. No random-direction baseline is given for the cosines.

versions.untested_parts: Toy-network superposition, sparsity-dependent transitions, and regular geometry.
Whether capacity pressure causes neuron polysemanticity or allocates dedicated dimensions to important features.
Polysemantic neurons and whether they arise without capacity pressure; the paper studies a refusal direction, not neurons.
Feature distribution across LLM neurons and recovery of sparse features with dictionaries or SAEs.
Whether SAE features are complete, stable, canonical units.
Whether represented features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: Qwen3-VL-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine similarity between the dirty refusal vector and the Logic concept atom.
rows.note: The paper presents this as evidence of entanglement between the refusal vector and a capability atom, not as a test of feature superposition.
rows.check: This is a cosine between a mean-difference refusal vector and a mean-difference concept atom. It says nothing about neuron polysemanticity or feature superposition. No baseline (e.g., random-direction cosine) is given, so 'observed' entanglement cannot be read against a control.

rows.subject: Qwen3-VL-2B
rows.operation_detail: Measured cosine similarity between the dirty refusal vector and the Coding concept atom.
rows.note: The paper presents this as evidence of entanglement between the refusal vector and a capability atom, not as a test of feature superposition.
rows.check: Same issue as R1: a vector-to-atom cosine with no baseline, which does not bear on any version.

rows.subject: not stated
rows.operation_detail: Compared projections of standard dirty and SRA-cleaned refusal vectors onto target, shield, and style-confound atoms.
rows.value: The text says standard ablation suppresses Shields nearly as strongly as refusal-related Targets, while SRA preserves Shields by removing their components from the intervention direction; numeric values not stated.
rows.note: The paper describes the figure's qualitative result but does not state a model or numeric projection values here.
rows.check: Subject is not stated in the Section 4.2 text. The result is figure-only and qualitative. It compares the study's own cleaned vector with the dirty one, so it is a method comparison rather than a measurement bearing on any version.
